title: Onigiri
subtitle: Japanese rice balls with tuna mayo filling
excerpt: Onigiri are Japanese hand-pressed rice balls, typically filled and wrapped in nori. The tuna mayo filling (maguro mayo) is the most popular convenience-store filling in Japan. They are eaten as a portable lunch, snack, or breakfast. The rice must be seasoned sushi rice for the characteristic flavour.
sourceNotes: Onigiri have been made in Japan since the Nara period (8th century). Originally plain salt-seasoned rice, they evolved to include fillings and nori wrapping in the Edo period. The tuna mayonnaise filling became popular in the 1980s following the convenience store revolution in Japan.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Wrap tightly in cling film. Best eaten within 4 hours.

content.text: Sushi rice is essential: the slight stickiness from the vinegar seasoning holds the onigiri together. Long-grain rice will not work. Wet your hands with salted water before shaping each onigiri. This prevents the rice sticking to your hands and seasons the outside. Press firmly: a loose onigiri falls apart.

items.prepNote: cooked and seasoned with rice vinegar and a pinch of sugar
nori sheets, cut into 3 strips each

content.text: Mix the drained tuna with mayonnaise and soy sauce. Season with salt if needed.

Wet your hands with cold salted water. Place about 80 g of warm cooked rice in one hand. Make a dent in the centre. Add 1 tablespoon of the tuna mayo. Cup both hands around the rice and press firmly into a triangle or ball shape, rotating and pressing 5 to 6 times until compact.
Wrap a strip of nori around the base of each onigiri. Serve immediately, or wrap tightly in cling film for up to 4 hours.

items.cause: Rice was not sticky enough or not pressed firmly
items.fix: Use proper sushi rice and press hard. The onigiri should feel solid, not hollow. If the rice is too cool and dry, it will not stick. Use it while still slightly warm.
